result.summary: The terrified Chorus of Theban women pray and imagine the sack of their city. The Scout reports the seven Argive champions at the seven gates, and Eteocles names a Theban defender for each of the first six. When he learns that his brother Polynices holds the seventh gate, he resolves to fight him himself despite the Chorus's pleas.

scenes.title: The Chorus fears the sack
scenes.summary: The Chorus prays to the gods to save Thebes and describes the horrors of a captured city.
scenes.stakes: The women fear slavery, violence and the destruction of their city if the gods abandon it.

scenes.title: Champions at six gates
scenes.summary: The Scout describes each Argive champion and his shield; Eteocles assigns a Theban to meet each of the first six.
scenes.stakes: Thebes risks capture at its seven gates; Eteocles must choose defenders well.

scenes.title: Eteocles resolves to fight Polynices
scenes.summary: Eteocles, mourning his father's curse, decides to face his brother at the seventh gate. The Chorus begs him to avoid kindred blood, but he refuses.
scenes.stakes: Eteocles risks death and the pollution of kindred bloodshed, fulfilling the curse of Oedipus.

notable_quotes.reason: The Scout's image of the ship of State is memorable.
Eteocles dismisses blazonry as powerless without the spear.
Amphiaraüs' blank shield: he wishes to be brave, not seem so.

analysis.text: The shield-devices pit words and symbols against deeds and justice, and Eteocles reads each as an omen. The catalogue builds toward the fated brother-against-brother duel.
The curse of Oedipus drives Eteocles toward self-destruction; fate and choice merge as he rejects the Chorus's warnings.

legacy.text: The shield catalogue, in which Aeschylus gives each gate a pair of champions, is a famous early example of dramatic ekphrasis and was echoed by later poets such as Euripides in the Phoenician Women.

fun_facts.text: Aristophanes' Frogs has Aeschylus boast that this play was full of the spirit of war, and the seven-gate scene is its centrepiece.

language_notes.text: "Fell" means cruel or deadly; "visitants" are the serpents that invade the dove's nest.
"Burghers" are the citizens of the town; here the Theban defenders on the walls.
Dirce is the spring near Thebes. Its waters are said to come from Poseidon and the Oceanid children of Tethys, a sea-goddess.
"Stablish" is archaic for establish; the Chorus asks the gods to remain securely in their seats (temples) at Thebes.
"Achaean" means Greek; here the Argive attackers are called Achaeans.
"I trow" is archaic for "I believe"; the dead are said to be better off than captives.
"Towering net of ruin" pictures conquest as a huge net cast over the city, trapping the people.
The bitterly ironic "nightly rite" means forced union with a conqueror; the sentence is dense and its sense is debated.
The Proetid gate is named for Proetus; the Ismenus is a river near Thebes. The seer Amphiaraus reads the sacrificial omens as unfavourable.
Oecles' son is the seer Amphiaraus. Tydeus taunts him for refusing to cross the river and fight.
Eteocles puns on the shield's emblem: if Tydeus dies, night falls on his eyes, so the device names his own fate.
The 'Heroes of the Dragon's blood' are the Sparti, who sprang from dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus; five survived, and Thebans claim descent from them.
'Ares with his dice' means war's outcome is a throw of chance; Justice is called Ares' kin because the cause is right.
'Giant' marks Capaneus as huge; 'him named afore' is Tydeus. 'Electran gate' is another of Thebes' seven gates.
Eteocles means that Capaneus's boasting is a second gain for Thebes, since arrogance against the gods invites ruin; 'with interest' continues the money metaphor.
"O'erweening" means arrogant or overbearing; the speaker prays the thunderbolt will stop the enemy before he plunders the women's quarters.
"Pipes in outlandish style": the horses' muzzle-gear whistles with their breath in a strange, foreign-sounding way.
"In words their letters frame": the boast is written on the shield as an inscription.
"Dragon's blood" refers to the Sparti, the armed men who sprang from dragon's teeth sown by Cadmus, ancestors of the Theban nobility.
Onca Athena is a Theban title of Athena; the gate named for her is the fourth.
Typhon was a fire-breathing monster who challenged Zeus and was defeated by him.
"Fitly hath Hermes confronted them": Hermes, god of luck and chance, is credited with the apt pairing of opponents.
"Maiden name": Parthenopaeus means "maiden-faced", which clashes with his fierce nature. The Sphinx was the monster that plagued Thebes until Oedipus solved her riddle.
"No petty trading" means he will not fight in a small, cheap way; the war is pictured as a market exchange.
Amphiaraüs blames Tydeus for urging the expedition; Adrastus is the king of Argos leading it.
The name Polynices means 'much strife'; Amphiaraüs dwells on the latter part, 'neikes' (strife), hinting that his quarrel is a curse. The footnote marks this.
'The mother's fount' means the motherland, Thebes, as a nourishing source; Polynices would dry it up by attacking it.
Amphiaraüs bears no blazon because he wishes to be brave rather than seem so; a famous line in the play.
'The road that is far to retrace' means a path from which return is hard; the Argives cannot easily retreat.
Loxias is a title of Apollo, god of prophecy, whose oracles foretold the doom of the Argive attackers.
'Blazon' is an emblem or device painted or fixed on a shield.
"So fitly named": Polynices means roughly "man of much strife" in Greek, so his name suits his quarrel with Thebes.
Blazonry means the emblems painted on his shield; here, a golden figure of Justice leading a man, with a boastful inscription.
Cadmeans are the Thebans, named for Cadmus, the city's legendary founder. Argives are the Greeks of Argos who attack with Polynices.
Pollution means the religious stain of kin-murder, which was believed to cling to a family and demand punishment across generations.
Cocytus is a river of the underworld; Eteocles wishes his family swept down to the realm of the dead.
The Avenging Spirit is the Erinys that pursues the family; the Chorus hopes sacrifice might lead it to leave the house.
Eteocles recalls dreams foretelling that brothers would divide their father's inheritance, meaning by the sword.

context_notes.text: Cadmus was Thebes' legendary founder, so "sons of Cadmus" means the Theban people.
Women of a sacked city were commonly enslaved in ancient warfare, as the Chorus here fears.
Eteocles, son of Oedipus, is king of Thebes and commands its defence against his brother Polynices and the Argive army.
Bells on shields were meant to terrify enemies with noise before the fighting began.
Polyphontes is a Theban defender; his name means 'much slaying'.
Lots were drawn from a helmet to assign each Argive champion a gate; this one falls to Eteoclus.
Amphion, son of Zeus, was a legendary builder of Thebes' walls; his tomb stood near the Northern gate.
Actor is the brother of Hyperbius, the Theban champion Eteocles named earlier.
Amphiaraüs was an Argive seer who foresaw his own death in this war but was forced to join it.
Oecles' son is Amphiaraüs. Eteocles pities him as a righteous man doomed by the company he keeps.
The seventh gate is where Polynices, Eteocles' brother, attacks. The brothers are sons of Oedipus and quarrel over the throne and exile.
Polynices' shield shows Justice leading him home, a claim the play treats ironically, since his attack on his own city is impious.
Oedipus, former king of Thebes, cursed his sons Eteocles and Polynices to divide their inheritance by the sword. The play enacts that curse.
Justice (Dike) was a goddess, daughter of Zeus, who upheld right order among gods and mortals.
Laius, father of Oedipus, had defied Apollo (Phoebus) by having a child, which began the family's doom.

literary_notes.text: The Chorus's fear is compared to a dove terrified for her nestlings, a image of helpless, protective anxiety.
Captive women dragged by the hair "like horses" strips them of dignity and shows the brutality of conquest.
Maidens "plucked all unripe" compares girls to fruit, stressing their youth and the violation of marriage rites.
War is described as mad and frenzied, defiling holiness, as though it were a wicked agent.
Tydeus's furious cries are likened to a serpent's hiss, painting him as venomous and bestial.
The star-filled sky with the full moon on Tydeus's shield displays his grandiose pride and, later, becomes an omen of death.
The comparison to a charger chafing at the bit conveys Tydeus's restless eagerness for battle.
Eteocles turns the boastful emblem into a prophecy of Tydeus's own death, making his vaunting self-condemning.
Capaneus defies Zeus's thunder, yet Eteocles expects the thunderbolt to strike him; his torch-emblem foreshadows the fire that will destroy him.
The horses' eagerness and the noisy gear give the whole attack a restless, menacing energy before any fighting begins.
Typhon on the shield expresses the attacker's monstrous, impious aim and his challenge to the gods.
Terror itself is said to make a boast at the gate, conveying how frightening the champion's shield seems.
Zeus on Hyperbius' shield opposes Typhon, so the shield images forecast the outcome of the duel.
Details of his downy cheeks and half-boy age portray Parthenopaeus as a youth of reckless, savage pride.
The seer's mind is a deeply ploughed field yielding wise counsel, contrasting his substance with the showy shields of others.
Eteocles' exclamation laments the unfairness of fate, framing a general moral reflection that he then applies to Amphiaraüs.
Infatuation is a field whose harvest is death; the farming imagery makes ruin a natural consequence of folly.
The just man sailing with villains, and being lashed by Heaven, illustrates how the innocent are destroyed with the guilty.
Polynices' shield shows Justice guiding him, though he attacks his homeland; the emblem ironically contradicts his actions.
The ship of State is a familiar image casting Eteocles as helmsman responsible for steering Thebes through danger.
Eteocles addresses the house of Oedipus directly, treating the doomed family as a single suffering being and opening the scene with lament.
Eteocles argues Justice would be false to her name if she sided with Polynices, unaware that his own course also meets the curse.
The repeated "against" in tight pairs builds a drumbeat of escalating opposition, ending on the shocking pairing of brother with foe.
Dry eyes that cannot weep, haunted by a curse that promises gain and then death, show his grief hardened into fate.
His closing line ends the debate with resignation, suggesting the curse has already settled the outcome.
